Pregnancy

Strong-smelling urine: causes, pregnancy considerations and when to get help

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A stronger urine smell can follow an ordinary change in food or fluids, but it can also occur alongside a health problem. Look at the whole pattern rather than using the smell alone to decide what is wrong.

A different smell is a clue, not a diagnosis

Urine normally has some smell, and its strength can change from one visit to the toilet to the next. Food, fluids, medicines and the length of time since you last passed urine can all contribute. A temporary change without other symptoms often has a straightforward explanation.

The description is subjective: one person may call an odour sweet, sharp or ammonia-like while another describes it differently. Do not use a smell chart to decide whether you have an infection, diabetes or liver disease. The accompanying symptoms, your health history and, when appropriate, testing are more useful.

Concentrated urine and dehydration

Urine can smell stronger when there is less water diluting its waste products. This may happen after several hours overnight, with reduced drinking, or during illness with fluid loss. An ammonia-like smell and a darker yellow colour can fit concentrated urine, but neither proves dehydration is the only cause.

Keep fluids available and drink regularly according to your needs and any medical advice. Thirst is a useful signal, not proof that you have already reached a dangerous level of dehydration. You do not need to force enough water to make urine completely colourless or odourless.

If you are vomiting, passing very little urine, becoming dizzy or struggling to keep fluids down, seek advice rather than only increasing a drinking target. During pregnancy, significant vomiting or signs of dehydration should be discussed with the maternity team. Follow any fluid restriction given for a heart or kidney condition.

Food changes, including asparagus

Asparagus is a familiar example of a food that can change urine odour. Its sulfur-containing compounds, including products formed when asparagusic acid is broken down, can produce a noticeable smell after eating it. This temporary effect does not in itself mean that the food has damaged the kidneys.

Other foods and drinks can also influence what you notice. Consider whether the change follows a particular meal and then settles. A food explanation is less reassuring if the smell continues without that exposure or appears with burning, fever, blood or pain. Those symptoms deserve attention even if you recently ate asparagus.

Review the exact medicine or supplement

Some medicines and supplements can alter urine odour; vitamin B6 is one recognised example. A pregnancy multivitamin may contain several ingredients, so bring the label or product name when asking for advice. Changes in urine colour and changes in smell are not necessarily caused by the same ingredient.

Do not assume all vitamin D products, B vitamins, sulfonamide antibiotics, diabetes medicines or rheumatoid-arthritis medicines have an identical effect. The ingredient, dose and formulation need checking. A broad medicine category is not enough to explain a new symptom safely.

Continue prescribed treatment unless the clinician advises otherwise. In particular, do not stop a recommended pregnancy supplement or diabetes medicine simply to test whether the smell disappears. A pharmacist can help assess a plausible side effect while identifying symptoms that need a medical review.

Urinary infection: symptoms matter more than smell

A urinary tract infection may cause a strong smell together with burning, urgency, frequent small amounts of urine, cloudy urine or lower abdominal discomfort. Blood may also be present. These symptoms can arise quickly and should not be dismissed because a similar smell previously followed food or a vitamin.

Antibiotics are used for an appropriate bacterial infection, but smell alone is not enough to select one. A clinician may request urine testing to establish what is happening and guide the choice. Avoid using leftover antibiotics or assuming that drinking more water will clear an infection that needs treatment.

Why pregnancy changes the assessment

A change in diet, supplements or hydration can affect urine during pregnancy. Pregnancy also changes the urinary tract through hormonal and mechanical effects; infection risk is not explained only by pressure on the bladder. Needing to urinate more often can be a normal pregnancy change, which makes a new painful or urgent pattern easy to overlook.

Contact your maternity clinician promptly if you suspect a UTI. Prenatal urine testing also looks for bacteria that may be present without obvious symptoms. The absence of a bad smell does not mean such testing is unnecessary, and an odour does not by itself establish the test result.

Follow the pregnancy-specific treatment and follow-up plan. Do not wait two days to see whether new urinary pain settles, and do not substitute a home remedy for a prescribed antibiotic. Tell the service how many weeks pregnant you are and whether fever, back pain or vomiting is present.

Fever or side pain can signal a more serious infection

Fever, chills, pain in the back or side, nausea, vomiting or feeling markedly unwell may indicate a kidney infection. This needs urgent assessment, especially during pregnancy. The smell may be strong, mild or unchanged; it is not a reliable measure of how far an infection has progressed.

Get emergency help for severe illness, confusion, collapse, breathing difficulty or inability to pass urine. If you cannot reach your maternity or primary-care team and symptoms are concerning, use local urgent or emergency care. Waiting for a particular odour or a fixed number of days can delay necessary treatment.

Diabetes and a sweet smell

High blood glucose can be associated with glucose in urine and a change described as sweet. However, smelling urine cannot establish diabetes or show whether existing diabetes is controlled. Increased thirst, passing larger amounts of urine, unexplained weight loss or persistent fatigue should prompt clinical assessment and appropriate tests.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is a different, urgent concern. Vomiting or abdominal pain together with unusual thirst, deep breathing, drowsiness, confusion or fruity-smelling breath needs emergency assessment. Fruity breath is not the same as an isolated urine odour. If you already have diabetes, follow your agreed illness and ketone-testing plan and seek help when advised.

A bowel-to-bladder fistula is an uncommon cause

A fistula is an abnormal connection between tissues or organs. If the bowel connects to the bladder, bowel contents and bacteria can enter the urinary tract. Repeated infections or unusual urine may lead a clinician to consider this possibility; passing gas or material resembling stool in urine is an especially useful symptom to report.

Possible causes include previous surgery, Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis and other bowel problems. Not every inflammatory bowel condition has the same fistula risk, and a strong smell by itself is not evidence of a fistula. Assessment usually needs attention to both the urinary tract and bowel rather than repeated treatment of odour alone.

Liver disease: look beyond an odour description

Liver disease should not be diagnosed from urine that seems sweet. More relevant changes can include dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes, fatigue, poor appetite, unintentional weight loss or abdominal swelling. Changes in sexual interest or function can occur in chronic illness but are not specific enough to identify a liver problem.

New jaundice or dark urine with other illness needs prompt assessment. Severe confusion, bleeding or collapse needs emergency care. These signs have several possible causes, so trying to decide which disease matches a smell can distract from symptoms that require examination and blood tests.

Phenylketonuria: a rare inherited condition

Phenylketonuria, or PKU, affects the body’s processing of phenylalanine, an amino acid obtained from protein. Without effective treatment, it can accumulate to harmful levels. A musty odour has been described, along with lighter pigmentation, developmental difficulties and behavioural or neurological problems in untreated disease.

These features are not a checklist for diagnosing a baby at home. Newborn screening and prompt follow-up can identify the condition before avoidable harm occurs. PKU requires ongoing specialist management, but calling it simply incurable misses the benefits of early treatment. A smell noticed for the first time in an otherwise well adult is not, by itself, a reason to assume PKU.

Maple syrup urine disease needs specialist care

Maple syrup urine disease is another rare inherited metabolic condition. The body cannot adequately break down the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. Their accumulation can be dangerous, and an odour resembling maple sugar may occur in urine or other body secretions.

An affected newborn may become unwell with poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting or abnormal movements. Severe untreated illness can damage the brain or be life-threatening. Screening, confirmatory testing and early specialist treatment are important; parents should not wait to recognise a smell.

Milder forms can become apparent later, but this remains a specialist diagnosis rather than a common explanation for adult urine odour. An abnormal screening result needs follow-up, not an immediate assumption that the diagnosis is certain. An unwell baby needs urgent assessment even before results are available.

Kidney stones and urinary blockage

Kidney stones are solid deposits that form in the kidneys and may move into the urinary tract. Some small stones cause few symptoms, while others lead to severe pain in the back, side, lower abdomen or groin. Pain when urinating, a constant urge to go, blood or unusual-smelling urine can accompany them.

Smell cannot tell you whether a stone is present, how large it is or whether it is obstructing urine flow. Severe pain, fever or chills, vomiting, or difficulty passing urine needs prompt assessment. Timely treatment often prevents lasting problems, but a blocked or infected urinary system should not be treated as harmless simply because stones are common.

Check whether the smell is coming from urine

An odour noticed while using the toilet may come from vaginal discharge, external skin or clothing rather than the urine itself. Tell the clinician about itching, soreness, changed discharge or another genital symptom. This can change the examination or sample needed.

During pregnancy, discharge that smells unusual or is accompanied by irritation should be discussed with your midwife or clinician. Avoid douching, scented sprays and vigorous washing to hide it. These measures do not treat an infection and can make irritated tissue more uncomfortable.

Support comfortable bladder habits

Use the toilet when you need to rather than routinely holding urine for long periods. A reminder every few hours, often around three to four during the day, can be useful for someone who forgets, but it is not a rule to force urine or drink excessively. Individual bladder plans and fluid restrictions take priority.

Allow time to relax and empty without rushing or straining. Regular movement within your abilities and adequate fluids support general bladder health. Breathable clothing, including cotton underwear if comfortable, can help keep the area dry; it is not a guarantee against infection or a treatment for an existing one.

If you feel unable to empty, have a persistently weak stream or repeatedly need to return to the toilet, ask for assessment. Do not respond only by sitting longer or pushing harder. A change in bladder function deserves attention even when the urine does not smell unusual.

What testing may involve

Assessment usually begins with the timing, associated symptoms, medicines, diet, fluids and pregnancy status. Urinalysis can check for several abnormalities; a urine culture looks for bacterial growth and may help guide treatment. A particular result must be interpreted in context, including how the sample was collected.

Cystoscopy uses a thin instrument with a camera to inspect the bladder. Imaging, such as ultrasound or another selected scan, may investigate stones, obstruction, recurrent infection or a suspected structural problem. Neither a camera test nor imaging is routine just because urine smells different. Persistent symptoms may justify further assessment even if an initial test is unrevealing.

When to arrange a review and what to bring

If an unexplained new smell continues, arrange a review and note when it began, any food or medicine changes, urine colour and accompanying symptoms. Persistent bloating, nausea or vomiting are worth mentioning, but they do not identify one particular disease. Bring relevant medical history and any recent urine-test or treatment results.

Do not apply a universal two-day waiting period to pain, blood, fever, pregnancy UTI symptoms or significant illness. Mild isolated odour and a temporary dietary explanation are different from a person who is unwell. The aim is to find a cause when necessary while avoiding diagnosis, antibiotics or invasive tests based on smell alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Food, concentrated urine and some medicines can affect odour. Smell alone does not diagnose infection or metabolic disease.

Suspected urinary infection during pregnancy needs prompt assessment. Kidney-infection symptoms or severe illness require urgent care.

How BeMama can help

Keep a short record of symptoms and recent product changes. Bring that information to the clinician rather than trying to match an odour to a disease online.

When to seek help

Maternity, primary-care and metabolic-topic review remain pending. Do not delay urgent care for an unwell adult or baby while waiting for a smell to change.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Consider diet, fluid intake and exact medicine ingredients without stopping prescribed treatment on your own.
  • Pregnancy screening can detect bacteria even when there is no smell or discomfort.
  • Fistulas, liver disease and inherited conditions require proper assessment; they are not diagnosed by odour.
  • A fixed two-day wait is inappropriate when warning symptoms are present.

Frequently asked questions

Is stronger morning urine always dehydration?

No. More concentrated urine after the night can smell stronger, but colour and smell cannot establish the only cause. Persistent change or other symptoms deserves review.

Can asparagus cause a smell without an infection?

Yes. Sulfur-containing breakdown products can temporarily change urine odour. Burning, fever, blood or pain still needs attention even after an asparagus-containing meal.

Should I stop pregnancy vitamins?

Do not stop a recommended supplement solely because of smell. Ask about the exact ingredients and product; some, such as vitamin B6, can affect odour.

Does sweet-smelling urine prove diabetes?

No. Diabetes is assessed with appropriate tests and symptoms. Unusual thirst or urine volume should be reviewed; vomiting, deep breathing, drowsiness or other ketoacidosis symptoms require emergency help.

Can a pregnancy urine test matter when I feel well?

Yes. Bacteria may be detected without symptoms. Follow the prenatal screening and treatment plan rather than relying on odour as a warning system.

Should I wait two days if urination burns during pregnancy?

No. Contact your maternity clinician promptly for suspected UTI. Fever, back or side pain, vomiting or marked illness needs urgent assessment.

What symptoms might suggest a bowel-to-bladder fistula?

Gas or stool-like material in urine and recurrent infections can be clues. A strong smell alone does not establish a fistula; clinical investigation is needed.

Can I identify PKU or maple syrup urine disease by smelling a nappy?

No. Screening and confirmatory tests are used. Follow up an abnormal screen promptly, and seek urgent care for a baby who feeds poorly or becomes unusually sleepy or unwell.

Will I need cystoscopy because my urine smells different?

Usually not for odour alone. A clinician chooses further tests for a specific concern, such as blood, repeated infection, obstruction or a structural problem.

Must I urinate exactly every three hours?

No. Avoid habitually delaying when you need to go, but follow your own bladder and fluid plan. Do not force urine or excessive drinking to meet a fixed timetable.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
